overview: A weak system brings light snow to the Cascades and Sierra over the weekend, then a short break Monday. A stronger, wetter system follows midweek (Tuesday to Wednesday) across the Pacific Northwest, B.C. and the Sierra.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: A weak system crosses the Cascades Saturday night into Sunday with light snow showers. The bulk of the moisture stays offshore, and the forecasters expect no impactful amounts. The next stronger system arrives Tuesday, bringing snow that turns to rain at lower levels, with Mt. Baker and Crystal Mountain getting the most. Stevens Pass sees its heaviest snow Tuesday.

regions.title: Tahoe
regions.text: Sunday brings a fast, weak system with light snow that is mostly done by Sunday night, and Monday is dry. The midweek storm is expected to be less wet and snowy than the last one. Sugar Bowl and Palisades are forecast the most snow, with Wednesday the peak day. Kirkwood sees its snow Wednesday.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Whistler and Cypress see little snow over the weekend, with flurries or showers in the mid-levels. Rain comes in more often through midweek, with the wettest and mildest air Tuesday and Wednesday. Snow stays limited, so expect soggy conditions at lower elevations.

regions.title: Eastern Sierra
regions.text: Sunday's system is fast-moving with little moisture, so snow levels stay low and totals stay modest, but it can still make the drive home difficult Sunday evening. Monday afternoon through Tuesday evening is the best travel window before Thanksgiving. Mammoth gets its strongest snow Wednesday, and winds will be gusty.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
